1 ἰοὺ ἰού·
2 ὦ Ζεῦ βασιλεῦ τὸ χρῆμα τῶν νυκτῶν ὅσον·
3 ἀπέραντον. οὐδέποθʼ ἡμέρα γενήσεται;
4 καὶ μὴν πάλαι γʼ ἀλεκτρυόνος ἤκουσʼ ἐγώ·
5 οἱ δʼ οἰκέται ῥέγκουσιν· ἀλλʼ οὐκ ἂν πρὸ τοῦ.
6 ἀπόλοιο δῆτʼ ὦ πόλεμε πολλῶν οὕνεκα,
7 ὅτʼ οὐδὲ κολάσʼ ἔξεστί μοι τοὺς οἰκέτας.
8 ἀλλʼ οὐδʼ ὁ χρηστὸς οὑτοσὶ νεανίας
9 ἐγείρεται τῆς νυκτός, ἀλλὰ πέρδεται
10 ἐν πέντε σισύραις ἐγκεκορδυλημένος.
11 ἀλλʼ εἰ δοκεῖ ῥέγκωμεν ἐγκεκαλυμμένοι.
12 ἀλλʼ οὐ δύναμαι δείλαιος εὕδειν δακνόμενος
13 ὑπὸ τῆς δαπάνης καὶ τῆς φάτνης καὶ τῶν χρεῶν
14 διὰ τουτονὶ τὸν υἱόν. ὁ δὲ κόμην ἔχων
15 ἱππάζεταί τε καὶ ξυνωρικεύεται
16 ὀνειροπολεῖ θʼ ἵππους· ἐγὼ δʼ ἀπόλλυμαι
17 ὁρῶν ἄγουσαν τὴν σελήνην εἰκάδας·
18 οἱ γὰρ τόκοι χωροῦσιν. ἅπτε παῖ λύχνον,
19 κἄκφερε τὸ γραμματεῖον, ἵνʼ ἀναγνῶ λαβὼν
20 ὁπόσοις ὀφείλω καὶ λογίσωμαι τοὺς τόκους.
21 φέρʼ ἴδω τί ὀφείλω; δώδεκα μνᾶς Πασίᾳ.
22 τοῦ δώδεκα μνᾶς Πασίᾳ; τί ἐχρησάμην;
23 ὅτʼ ἐπριάμην τὸν κοππατίαν. οἴμοι τάλας,
24 εἴθʼ ἐξεκόπην πρότερον τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν λίθῳ.
25 Φίλων ἀδικεῖς· ἔλαυνε τὸν σαυτοῦ δρόμον.
26 τοῦτʼ ἔστι τουτὶ τὸ κακὸν ὅ μʼ ἀπολώλεκεν·
27 ὀνειροπολεῖ γὰρ καὶ καθεύδων ἱππικήν.

0 1 Ah me! Ah me! O King Jupiter, of what a terrible length the nights are! Will it never be day? And yet long since I heard the cock. 5 My domestics are snoring; but they would not have done so heretofore! May you perish then, O war! For many reasons; because I may not even punish my domestics. Neither does this excellent youth awake through the night; but takes his ease, 10 wrapped up in five blankets. Well, if it is the fashion, let us snore wrapped up. 12 But I am not able, miserable man, to sleep, being tormented by my expenses, and my stud of horses, and my debts, through this son of mine. He with his long hair, 15 is riding horses and driving curricles, and dreaming of horses; while I am driven to distraction, as I see the moon bringing on the twentieths; for the interest is running on. Boy! Light a lamp, and bring forth my tablets, that I may take them and read 20 to how many I am indebted, and calculate the interest. Enter boy with a light and tablets. Come, let me see; what do I owe? Twelve minae to Pasias. Why twelve minae to Pasias? Why did I borrow them? When I bought the blood-horse. Ah me, unhappy! Would that it had had its eye knocked out with a stone first! 25 You are acting unfairly, Philo! Drive on your own course. 26 This is the bane that has destroyed me; for even in his sleep he dreams about horsemanship. 28 How many courses will the war-chariots run? 29 Many courses do you drive me, your father. But what debt came upon me after Pasias? Three minae to Amynias for a little chariot and pair of wheels. 32 Lead the horse home, after having given him a good rolling. 33 O foolish youth, you have rolled me out of my possessions; since I have been cast in suits, and others say that they will have surety given them for the interest. 35b Pray, father, why are you peevish, and toss about the whole night? 37 A bailiff out of the bedclothes is biting me. 38 Suffer me, good sir, to sleep a little. 39 Then, do you sleep on; but know that all these debts will turn on your head. Phidippides falls asleep again. Alas! Would that the match-maker had perished miserably, who induced me to marry your mother. For a country life used to be most agreeable to me, dirty, untrimmed, reclining at random, 45 abounding in bees, and sheep, and oil-cake. Then I, a rustic, married a niece of Megacles, the son of Megacles, from the city, haughty, luxurious, and Coesyrafied. When I married her, I lay with her 50 redolent of new wine, of the cheese-crate, and abundance of wool; but she, on the contrary, of ointment, saffron, wanton-kisses, extravagance, gluttony, and of Colias and Genetyllis. I will not indeed say that she was idle; but she wove. And I used to show her this cloak 55 by way of a pretext and say Wife, you weave at a great rate. 56 We have no oil in the lamp. 57 Ah me! Why did you light the thirsty lamp? Come hither that you may weep! 58b For what, pray, shall I weep? 59 Because you put in one of the thick wicks. 60 After this, when this son was born to us, to me, forsooth, and to my excellent wife, we squabbled then about the name: for she was for adding hippos to the name, Xanthippus, or Charippus, or Callipides; 65 but I was for giving him the name of his grandfather, Phidonides. For a time therefore we disputed; and then at length we agreed, and called him Phidippides. She used to take this son and fondle him, saying, When you, being grown up, shall drive your chariot to the city, 70 like Megacles, with a xystis. But I used to say, Nay, rather, when dressed in a leathern jerkin, you shall drive goats from Phelleus, like your father. He paid no attention to my words, but poured a horse-fever over my property. 75 Now, therefore, by meditating the whole night, I have discovered one path for my course extraordinarily excellent; to which if I persuade this youth I shall be saved. But first I wish to awake him. How then can I awake him in the most agreeable manner? How? 80 Phidippides, my little Phidippides? 80b What, father?

30 ἀτὰρ τί χρέος ἔβα με μετὰ τὸν Πασίαν;
31 τρεῖς μναῖ διφρίσκου καὶ τροχοῖν Ἀμυνίᾳ.
32 ἄπαγε τὸν ἵππον ἐξαλίσας οἴκαδε.
33 ἀλλʼ ὦ μέλʼ ἐξήλικας ἐμέ γʼ ἐκ τῶν ἐμῶν,
34 ὅτε καὶ δίκας ὤφληκα χἄτεροι τόκου
35 ἐνεχυράσεσθαί φασιν.
35b ἐτεὸν ὦ πάτερ
36 τί δυσκολαίνεις καὶ στρέφει τὴν νύχθʼ ὅλην;
37 δάκνει μὲ δήμαρχός τις ἐκ τῶν στρωμάτων.
38 ἔασον ὦ δαιμόνιε καταδαρθεῖν τί με.
39 σὺ δʼ οὖν κάθευδε· τὰ δὲ χρέα ταῦτʼ ἴσθʼ ὅτι
40 ἐς τὴν κεφαλὴν ἅπαντα τὴν σὴν τρέψεται.
41 φεῦ.
41a εἴθʼ ὤφελʼ ἡ προμνήστριʼ ἀπολέσθαι κακῶς,
42 ἥτις με γῆμʼ ἐπῆρε τὴν σὴν μητέρα·
43 ἐμοὶ γὰρ ἦν ἄγροικος ἥδιστος βίος
44 εὐρωτιῶν, ἀκόρητος, εἰκῇ κείμενος,
45 βρύων μελίτταις καὶ προβάτοις καὶ στεμφύλοις.
46 ἔπειτʼ ἔγημα Μεγακλέους τοῦ Μεγακλέους
47 ἀδελφιδῆν ἄγροικος ὢν ἐξ ἄστεως,
48 σεμνὴν τρυφῶσαν ἐγκεκοισυρωμένην.
49 ταύτην ὅτʼ ἐγάμουν, συγκατεκλινόμην ἐγὼ
50 ὄζων τρυγὸς τρασιᾶς ἐρίων περιουσίας,
51 ἡ δʼ αὖ μύρου κρόκου καταγλωττισμάτων,
52 δαπάνης λαφυγμοῦ Κωλιάδος Γενετυλλίδος.
53 οὐ μὴν ἐρῶ γʼ ὡς ἀργὸς ἦν, ἀλλʼ ἐσπάθα.
54 ἐγὼ δʼ ἂν αὐτῇ θοἰμάτιον δεικνὺς τοδὶ
55 πρόφασιν ἔφασκον, ὦ γύναι λίαν σπαθᾷς.
56 ἔλαιον ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔνεστʼ ἐν τῷ λύχνῳ.
57 οἴμοι· τί γάρ μοι τὸν πότην ἧπτες λύχνον;

58 δεῦρʼ ἔλθʼ ἵνα κλάῃς.
58b διὰ τί δῆτα κλαύσομαι;
59 ὅτι τῶν παχειῶν ἐνετίθεις θρυαλλίδων.
60 μετὰ ταῦθʼ, ὅπως νῷν ἐγένεθʼ υἱὸς οὑτοσί,
61 ἐμοί τε δὴ καὶ τῇ γυναικὶ τἀγαθῇ,
62 περὶ τοὐνόματος δὴ ʼντεῦθεν ἐλοιδορούμεθα·
63 ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἵππον προσετίθει πρὸς τοὔνομα,
64 Ξάνθιππον ἤ Χαριππον ἢ Καλλιππίδην,
65 ἐγὼ δὲ τοῦ πάππου ʼτιθέμην Φειδωνίδην.
66 τέως μὲν οὖν ἐκρινόμεθʼ· εἶτα τῷ χρόνῳ
67 κοινῇ ξυνέβημεν κἀθέμεθα Φειδιππίδην.
68 τοῦτον τὸν υἱὸν λαμβάνουσʼ ἐκορίζετο,
69 ὅταν σὺ μέγας ὢν ἅρμʼ ἐλαύνῃς πρὸς πόλιν,
70 ὥσπερ Μεγακλέης, ξυστίδʼ ἔχων. ἐγὼ δʼ ἔφην,
71 ὅταν μὲν οὖν τὰς αἶγας ἐκ τοῦ φελλέως,
72 ὥσπερ ὁ πατήρ σου, διφθέραν ἐνημμένος.
73 ἀλλʼ οὐκ ἐπίθετο τοῖς ἐμοῖς οὐδὲν λόγοις,
74 ἀλλʼ ἵππερόν μου κατέχεεν τῶν χρημάτων.
75 νῦν οὖν ὅλην τὴν νύκτα φροντίζων ὁδοῦ
76 μίαν ηὗρον ἀτραπὸν δαιμονίως ὑπερφυᾶ,
77 ἣν ἢν ἀναπείσω τουτονί, σωθήσομαι.
78 ἀλλʼ ἐξεγεῖραι πρῶτον αὐτὸν βούλομαι.
79 πῶς δῆτʼ ἂν ἥδιστʼ αὐτὸν ἐπεγείραιμι; πῶς;
80 Φειδιππίδη Φειδιππίδιον.
80b τί ὦ πάτερ;
81 κύσον με καὶ τὴν χεῖρα δὸς τὴν δεξιάν.
82 ἰδού. τί ἔστιν;
82b εἰπέ μοι, φιλεῖς ἐμέ;
83 νὴ τὸν Ποσειδῶ τουτονὶ τὸν ἵππιον.
84 μὴ ʼμοί γε τοῦτον μηδαμῶς τὸν ἵππιον·

81 Kiss me, and give me your right hand! 82 There. What’s the matter? 82b Tell me, do you love me? 83 Yes, by this Equestrian Neptune. 84 Nay, do not by any means mention this Equestrian to me, for this god is the author of my misfortunes. But, if you really love me from your heart, my son, obey me. 87b In what then, pray, shall I obey you? 88 Reform your habits as quickly as possible, and go and learn what I advise. 90 Tell me now, what do you prescribe? 90b And will you obey me at all? 90c By Bacchus, I will obey you. 91b Look this way then! Do you see this little door and little house? 93 I see it. What then, pray, is this, father? 94 This is a thinking-shop of wise spirits. 95 There dwell men who in speaking of the heavens persuade people that it is an oven, and that it encompasses us, and that we are the embers. These men teach, if one give them money, to conquer in speaking, right or wrong. 100 Who are they? 100b I do not know the name accurately. They are minute philosophers, noble and excellent. 103 Bah! They are rogues; I know them. You mean the quacks, the pale-faced wretches, the bare-footed fellows, of whose numbers are the miserable Socrates and Chaerephon. 105 Hold! Hold! Be silent! Do not say anything foolish. But, if you have any concern for your father’s patrimony, become one of them, having given up your horsemanship. 108 I would not, by Bacchus, even if you were to give me the pheasants which Leogoras rears! 110 Go, I entreat you, dearest of men, go and be taught. 111b Why, what shall I learn? 112 They say that among them are both the two causes—the better cause, whichever that is, and the worse: they say that the one of these two causes, the worse, prevails, 115 though it speaks on the unjust side. If, therefore you learn for me this unjust cause, I would not pay any one, not even an obolus of these debts, which I owe at present on your account. 119 I can not comply; for I should not dare to look upon the knights, having lost all my colour. 121 Then, by Ceres, you shall not eat any of my good! Neither you, nor your blood-horse; but I will drive you out of my house to the crows. 124 My uncle Megacles will not permit me to be without a horse. But I’ll go in, and pay no heed to you. 126 Though fallen, still I will not lie prostrate: but having prayed to the gods, I will go myself to the thinking-shop and get taught. How, then, being an old man, 130 shall I learn the subtleties of refined disquisitions? I must go. Why thus do I loiter and not knock at the door? Knocks at the door. Boy! Little boy! 133 Go to the devil! Who it is that knocked at the door? 134 Strepsiades, the son of Phidon, of Cicynna.

85 οὗτος γὰρ ὁ θεὸς αἴτιός μοι τῶν κακῶν.
86 ἀλλʼ εἴπερ ἐκ τῆς καρδίας μʼ ὄντως φιλεῖς,
87 ὦ παῖ πιθοῦ.
87b τί οὖν πίθωμαι δῆτά σοι;
88 ἔκστρεψον ὡς τάχιστα τοὺς σαυτοῦ τρόπους,
89 καὶ μάνθανʼ ἐλθὼν ἃν ἐγὼ παραινέσω.
90 λέγε δή, τί κελεύεις;
90b καί τι πείσει;
90c πείσομαι
91 νὴ τὸν Διόνυσον.
91b δεῦρό νυν ἀπόβλεπε.
92 ὁρᾷς τὸ θύριον τοῦτο καὶ τᾠκίδιον;
93 ὁρῶ. τί οὖν τοῦτʼ ἐστὶν ἐτεὸν ὦ πάτερ;
94 ψυχῶν σοφῶν τοῦτʼ ἐστὶ φροντιστήριον.
95 ἐνταῦθʼ ἐνοικοῦσʼ ἄνδρες, οἳ τὸν οὐρανὸν
96 λέγοντες ἀναπείθουσιν ὡς ἔστιν πνιγεύς,
97 κἄστιν περὶ ἡμᾶς οὗτος, ἡμεῖς δʼ ἄνθρακες.
98 οὗτοι διδάσκουσʼ, ἀργύριον ἤν τις διδῷ,
99 λέγοντα νικᾶν καὶ δίκαια κἄδικα.
100 εἰσὶν δὲ τίνες;
100b οὐκ οἶδʼ ἀκριβῶς τοὔνομα·
102 μεριμνοφροντισταὶ καλοί τε κἀγαθοί.
103 αἰβοῖ πονηροί γʼ, οἶδα. τοὺς ἀλαζόνας
104 τοὺς ὠχριῶντας τοὺς ἀνυποδήτους λέγεις,
105 ὧν ὁ κακοδαίμων Σωκράτης καὶ Χαιρεφῶν.
105b ἢ ἢ σιώπα· μηδὲν εἴπῃς νήπιον.
106 ἀλλʼ εἴ τι κήδει τῶν πατρῴων ἀλφίτων,
107 τούτων γενοῦ μοι σχασάμενος τὴν ἱππικήν.

109 τοὺς φασιανοὺς οὓς τρέφει Λεωγόρας.

111 ἐλθὼν διδάσκου.
111b καὶ τί σοι μαθήσομαι;
112 εἶναι παρʼ αὐτοῖς φασιν ἄμφω τὼ λόγω,
113 τὸν κρείττονʼ, ὅστις ἐστί, καὶ τὸν ἥττονα.
114 τούτοιν τὸν ἕτερον τοῖν λόγοιν, τὸν ἥττονα,
115 νικᾶν λέγοντά φασι τἀδικώτερα.
116 ἢν οὖν μάθῃς μοι τὸν ἄδικον τοῦτον λόγον,
117 ἃ νῦν ὀφείλω διὰ σέ, τούτων τῶν χρεῶν
118 οὐκ ἂν ἀποδοίην οὐδʼ ἂν ὀβολὸν οὐδενί.
119 οὐκ ἂν πιθοίμην· οὐ γὰρ ἂν τλαίην ἰδεῖν
120 τοὺς ἱππέας τὸ χρῶμα διακεκναισμένος.
121 οὐκ ἄρα μὰ τὴν Δήμητρα τῶν γʼ ἐμῶν ἔδει,
122 οὔτʼ αὐτὸς οὔθʼ ὁ ζύγιος οὔθʼ ὁ σαμφόρας·
123 ἀλλʼ ἐξελῶ σʼ ἐς κόρακας ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας.
124 ἀλλʼ οὐ περιόψεταί μʼ ὁ θεῖος Μεγακλέης
125 ἄνιππον. ἀλλʼ εἴσειμι, σοῦ δʼ οὐ φροντιῶ.
126 ἀλλʼ οὐδʼ ἐγὼ μέντοι πεσών γε κείσομαι,
127 ἀλλʼ εὐξάμενος τοῖσιν θεοῖς διδάξομαι
128 αὐτὸς βαδίζων ἐς τὸ φροντιστήριον.
129 πῶς οὖν γέρων ὢν κἀπιλήσμων καὶ βραδὺς
130 λόγων ἀκριβῶν σχινδαλάμους μαθήσομαι;
131 ἰτητέον. τί ταῦτʼ ἔχων στραγγεύομαι,
132 ἀλλʼ οὐχὶ κόπτω τὴν θύραν; παῖ παιδίον.
133 βάλλʼ ἐς κόρακας· τίς ἐσθʼ ὁ κόψας τὴν θύραν;
134 Φείδωνος υἱὸς Στρεψιάδης Κικυννόθεν.
135 ἀμαθής γε νὴ Δίʼ ὅστις οὑτωσὶ σφόδρα
136 ἀπεριμερίμνως τὴν θύραν λελάκτικας
137 καὶ φροντίδʼ ἐξήμβλωκας ἐξηυρημένην.
138 σύγγνωθί μοι· τηλοῦ γὰρ οἰκῶ τῶν ἀγρῶν.

135 You are a stupid fellow, by Jove! who have kicked against the door so very carelessly, and have caused the miscarriage of an idea which I had conceived. 138 Pardon me; for I dwell afar in the country. But tell me the thing which has been made to miscarry. 140 It is not lawful to mention it, except to disciples. 141 Tell it, then, to me without fear; for I here am come as a disciple to the thinking-shop. 143 I will tell you; but you must regard these as mysteries. Socrates lately asked Chaerephon about a flea, how many of its own feet it jumped; for after having bit the eyebrow of Chaerephon, it leaped away onto the head of Socrates. 148 How then did he measure this? 148b Most cleverly. He melted some wax; and then took the flea 150 and dipped its feet in the wax; and then a pair of Persian slippers stuck to it when cooled. Having gently loosened these, he measured back the distance. 153 O King Jupiter! What subtlety of thought! 154 What then would you say if you heard another contrivance of Socrates? 155b Of what kind? Tell me, I beseech you! 156 Chaerephon the Sphettian asked him whether he thought gnats buzzed through the mouth or the breech. 159 What, then, did he say about the gnat? 160 He said the intestine of the gnat was narrow and that the wind went forcibly through it, being slender, straight to the breech; and then that the rump, being hollow where it is adjacent to the narrow part, resounded through the violence of the wind. 165 The rump of the gnats then is a trumpet! Oh, thrice happy he for his sharp-sightedness! Surely a defendant might easily get acquitted who understands the intestine of the gnat. 169 But he was lately deprived of a great idea by a lizard. 170b In what way? Tell me. 171 As he was investigating the courses of the moon and her revolutions, then as he was gaping upward a lizard in the darkness dropped upon him from the roof. 174 I am amused at a lizard’s having dropped on Socrates. 175 Yesterday evening there was no supper for us. 176 Well. What then did he contrive for provisions? 177 He sprinkled fine ashes on the table, and bent a little spit, and then took it as a pair of compasses and filched a cloak from the Palaestra. 180 Why then do we admire Thales? Open open quickly the thinking-shop, and show to me Socrates as quickly as possible. For I desire to be a disciple. Come, open the door. The door of the thinking-shop opens and the pupils of Socrates are seen all with their heads fixed on the ground, while Socrates himself is seen suspended in the air in a basket. O Hercules, from what country are these wild beasts? 185 What do you wonder at? To what do they seem to you to be like? 186 To the Spartans who were taken at Pylos. But why in the world do these look upon the ground? 188 They are in search of the things below the earth. 188b Then they are searching for roots. Do not, then, trouble yourselves about this; 190 for I know where there are large and fine ones. Why, what are these doing, who are bent down so much? 192 These are groping about in darkness under Tartarus. 193 Why then does their rump look toward heaven?

139 ἀλλʼ εἰπέ μοι τὸ πρᾶγμα τοὐξημβλωμένον.
140 ἀλλʼ οὐ θέμις πλὴν τοῖς μαθηταῖσιν λέγειν.

142 ἥκω μαθητὴς ἐς τὸ φροντιστήριον.
143 λέξω. νομίσαι δὲ ταῦτα χρὴ μυστήρια.

145 ψύλλαν ὁπόσους ἅλλοιτο τοὺς αὑτῆς πόδας·

148 πῶς δῆτα διεμέτρησε;

150 ἐνέβαψεν ἐς τὸν κηρὸν αὐτῆς τὼ πόδε,

153 ὦ Ζεῦ βασιλεῦ τῆς λεπτότητος τῶν φρενῶν.
154 τί δῆτʼ ἂν ἕτερον εἰ πύθοιο Σωκράτους
155 φρόντισμα;
155b ποῖον; ἀντιβολῶ κάτειπέ μοι.
156 ἀνήρετʼ αὐτὸν Χαιρεφῶν ὁ Σφήττιος
157 ὁπότερα τὴν γνώμην ἔχοι, τὰς ἐμπίδας
158 κατὰ τὸ στόμʼ ᾄδειν ἢ κατὰ τοὐρροπύγιον.
159 τί δῆτʼ ἐκεῖνος εἶπε περὶ τῆς ἐμπίδος;

314 Tell me, O Socrates, I beseech you, by Jupiter, who are these that have uttered this grand song? Are they some heroines? 316 By no means; but heavenly Clouds, great divinities to idle men; who supply us with thought and argument, and intelligence and humbug, and circumlocution, and ability to hoax, and comprehension. 319 On this account therefore my soul, having heard their voice, flutters, and already seeks to discourse subtilely, and to quibble about smoke, and having pricked a maxim with a little notion, to refute the opposite argument. So that now I eagerly desire, if by any means it be possible, to see them palpably. 323 Look, then, hither, toward Mount Parnes; for now I behold them descending gently. 324b Pray where? Show me. 324c See! There they come in great numbers through the hollows and thickets; there, obliquely. 325b What’s the matter? For I can’t see them. 326b By the entrance. 326c Now at length with difficulty I just see them. 327 Now at length you assuredly see them, unless you have your eyes running pumpkins. 328 Yes, by Jupiter! O highly honoured Clouds, for now they cover all things. 329 Did you not, however, know, nor yet consider, these to be goddesses? 330 No, by Jupiter! But I thought them to be mist, and dew, and smoke. 331 For you do not know, by Jupiter! that these feed very many sophists, Thurian soothsayers, practisers of medicine, lazy-long-haired-onyx-ring-wearers, song-twisters for the cyclic dances, and meteorological quacks. They feed idle people who do nothing, because such men celebrate them in verse. 335 For this reason, then, they introduced into their verses the dreadful impetuosity of the moist, whirling-bright clouds; and the curls of hundred-headed Typho; and the hard-blowing tempests; and then aerial, moist; crooked-clawed birds, floating in air and the showers of rain from dewy Clouds. And then, in return for these, they swallow slices of great, fine mullets, and bird’s-flesh of thrushes. 340 Is it not just, however, that they should have their reward, on account of these? 340b Tell me, pray, if they are really clouds, what ails them, that they resemble mortal women? For they are not such. 342b Pray, of what nature are they? 343 I do not clearly know: at any rate they resemble spread-out fleeces, and not women, by Jupiter! Not a bit; for these have noses. 345 Answer, then, whatever I ask you. 345b Then say quickly what you wish. 346 Have you ever, when you; looked up, seen a cloud like to a centaur, or a panther, or a wolf, or a bull? 347b By Jupiter, have I! But what of that? 348 They become all things, whatever they please. And then if they see a person with long hair, a wild one of these hairy fellows, like the son of Xenophantes, in derision of his folly, they liken themselves to centaurs. 351 Why, what, if they should see Simon, a plunderer of the public property, what do they do? 352 They suddenly become wolves, showing up his disposition. 353 For this reason, then, for this reason, when they yesterday saw Cleonymus the recreant, on this account they became stags, because they saw this most cowardly fellow. 355 And now too, because they saw Clisthenes, you observe, on this account they became women.

356 Hail therefore, O mistresses! And now, if ever ye did to any other, to me also utter a voice reaching to heaven, O all-powerful queens. 358 Hail, O ancient veteran, hunter after learned speeches! And thou, O priest of most subtle trifles! Tell us what you require? 360 For we would not hearken to any other of the recent meteorological sophists, except to Prodicus; to him, on account of his wisdom and intelligence; and to you, because you walk proudly in the streets, and cast your eyes askance, and endure many hardships with bare feet, and in reliance upon us lookest supercilious. 364 O Earth, what a voice! How holy and dignified and wondrous! 365 For, in fact, these alone are goddesses; and all the rest is nonsense. 366 But come, by the Earth, is not Jupiter, the Olympian, a god? 367 What Jupiter? Do not trifle. There is no Jupiter. 367b What do you say? Who rains then? For first of all explain this to me. 369 These to be sure. I will teach you it by powerful evidence. Come, where have you ever seen him raining at any time without Clouds? And yet he ought to rain in fine weather, and these be absent. 372 By Apollo, of a truth you have rightly confirmed this by your present argument. And yet, before this, I really thought that Jupiter caused the rain. But tell me who is it that thunders. This makes me tremble. 375 These, as they roll, thunder. 375b In what way? you all-daring man! 376 When they are full of much water, and are compelled to be borne along, being necessarily precipitated when full of rain, then they fall heavily upon each other and burst and clap. 379 Who is it that compels them to borne along? Is it not Jupiter? 380 By no means, but aethereal Vortex. 380b Vortex? It had escaped my notice that Jupiter did not exist, and that Vortex now reigned in his stead. But you have taught me nothing as yet concerning the clap and the thunder. 383 Have you not heard me, that I said that the Clouds, when full of moisture, dash against each other and clap by reason of their density? 385 Come, how am I to believe this? 385b I’ll teach you from your own case. Were you ever, after being stuffed with broth at the Panathenaic festival, then disturbed in your belly, and did a tumult suddenly rumble through it? 388 Yes, by Apollo! And immediately the little broth plays the mischief with me, and is disturbed and rumbles like thunder, and grumbles dreadfully: 390 at first gently pappax, pappax; and then it adds papa-pappax; and finally, it thunders downright papapappax, as they do. 392 Consider, therefore, how you have trumpeted from a little belly so small; and how is it not probable that this air, being boundless, should thunder so loudly? 394 For this reason, therefore, the two names also Trump and Thunder, are similar to each other. But teach me this, whence comes the thunderbolt blazing with fire, and burns us to ashes when it smites us, and singes those who survive. For indeed Jupiter evidently hurls this at the perjured. 398 Why, how then, you foolish person, and savouring of the dark ages and antediluvian, if his manner is to smite the perjured, does he not blast Simon, 400 and Cleonymus, and Theorus? And yet they are very perjured. But he smites his own temple, and Sunium the promontory of Athens, and the tall oaks. Wherefore, for indeed an oak does not commit perjury. 403 I do not know; but you seem to speak well. For what, pray, is the thunderbolt? 404 When a dry wind, having been raised aloft, is inclosed in these Clouds, it inflates them within, like a bladder; and then, of necessity, having burst them, it rushes out with vehemence by reason of its density, setting fire to itself through its rushing and impetuosity. 408 By Jupiter, of a truth I once experienced this exactly at the Diasian festival! I was roasting a haggis for my kinsfolk, and through neglect I did not cut it open; but it became inflated and then suddenly bursting, befouled my eyes and burned my face. 412 O mortal, who hast desired great wisdom from us! How happy will you become among the Athenians and among the Greeks, if you be possessed of a good memory, and be a deep thinker, and endurance of labour be implanted 415 in your soul, and you be not wearied either by standing or walking, nor be exceedingly vexed at shivering with cold, nor long to break your fast, and you refrain from wine, and gymnastics, and the other follies, and consider this the highest excellence, as is proper a clever man should, to conquer by action and counsel, and by battling with your tongue. 420 As far as regards a sturdy spirit, and care that makes one’s bed uneasy, and a frugal spirit and hard-living and savory-eating belly, be of good courage and don’t trouble yourself; I would offer myself to hammer on, for that matter. 423 Will you not, pray, now believe in no god, except what we believe in--this Chaos, and the Clouds, and the Tongue--these three? 425 Absolutely I would not even converse with the others, not even if I met them; nor would I sacrifice to them, nor make libations, nor offer frankincense. 427 Tell us then boldly, what we must do for you? For you shall not fail in getting it, if you honour and admire us, and seek to become clever. 429 O mistresses, I request of you then this very small favour, that I be the best of the Greeks in speaking by a hundred stadia. 431 Well, you shall have this from us, so that hence-forward from this time no one shall get more opinions passed in the public assemblies than you. 433 Grant me not to deliver important opinions; for I do not desire these, but only to pervert the right for my own advantage, and to evade my creditors. 435 Then you shall obtain what you desire; for you do not covet great things. But commit yourself without fear to our ministers. 437 I will do so in reliance upon you, for necessity oppresses me, on account of the blood-horses, and the marriage that ruined me. Now, therefore, let them use me as they please. 440 I give up this body to them to be beaten, to be hungered, to be troubled with thirst, to be squalid, to shiver with cold, to flay into a leathern bottle, 445 if I shall escape clear from my debts, and appear to men to be bold, glib of tongue, audacious, impudent, shameless, a fabricator of falsehoods, inventive of words, a practiced knave in lawsuits, a law-tablet, a thorough rattle, a fox, a sharper, a slippery knave, a dissembler, a slippery fellow, an impostor, 450 a gallows-bird, a blackguard, a twister, a troublesome fellow, a licker-up of hashes. If they call me this, when they meet me, let them do to me absolutely what they please. And if they like, 455 by Ceres, let them serve up a sausage out of me to the deep thinkers.

478 Come now, tell me your own turn of mind; in order that, when I know of what sort it is, I may now, after this, apply to you new engines. 481 What? By the gods, do you purpose to besiege me? 482 No; I wish to briefly learn from you if you are possessed of a good memory. 483b In two ways, by Jove! If anything be owing to me, I have a very good memory; but if I owe unhappy man, I am very forgetful. 486 Is the power of speaking, pray, implanted in your nature? 487 Speaking is not in me, but cheating is. 488 How, then, will you be able to learn? 488b Excellently, of course. 489 Come, then, take care that, whenever I propound any clever dogma about abstruse matters, you catch it up immediately. 491 What then? Am I to feed upon wisdom like a dog? 492 This man is ignorant and brutish--I fear, old man, lest you will need blows. Come, let me see; what do you do if any one beat you? 494b I take the beating; and then, when I have waited a little while, I call witnesses to prove it; then again, after a short interval, I go to law. 497 Come, then, lay down your cloak. 497b Have I done any wrong? 498 No; but it is the rule to enter naked. 499 But I do not enter to search for stolen goods. 500 Lay it down. Why do you talk nonsense? 500b Now tell me this, pray. 501 If I be diligent and learn zealously, to which of your disciples shall I become like? 503 You will no way differ from Chaerephon in intellect. 504 Ah me, unhappy! I shall become half-dead. 505 Don’t chatter; but quickly follow me hither with smartness. 506b Then give me first into my hands a honeyed cake; for I am afraid of descending within, as if into the cave of Trophonius. 509 Proceed; why do you keep poking about the door?

961 I will, therefore, describe the ancient system of education, how it was ordered, when I flourished in the advocacy of justice, and temperance was the fashion. In the first place it was incumbent that no one should hear the voice of a boy uttering a syllable; and next, that those from the same quarter of the town should march in good order through the streets to the school of the harp-master, 965 naked, and in a body, even if it were to snow as thick as meal. Then again, their master would teach them, not sitting cross-legged, to learn by rote a song, either Παλλάδα περσέπολιν δεινὰν or τηλέπορόν τι βόαμα raising to a higher pitch the harmony which our fathers transmitted to us. But if any of them were to play the buffoon, or to turn any quavers, 970 like these difficult turns the present artists make after the manner of Phrynis, he used to be thrashed, being beaten with many blows, as banishing the Muses. And it behooved the boys, while sitting in the school of the Gymnastic-master, to cover the thigh, so that they might exhibit nothing indecent to those outside; 975 then again, after rising from the ground, to sweep the sand together, and to take care not to leave an impression of the person for their lovers. And no boy used in those days to anoint himself below the navel; so that their bodies wore the appearance of blooming health. Nor used he to go to his lover, having made up his voice in an effeminate tone, 980 prostituting himself with his eyes. Nor used it to be allowed when one was dining to take the head of the radish, or to snatch from their seniors dill or parsley, or to eat fish, or to giggle, or to keep the legs crossed. 984 Aye, antiquated and dipolia-like and full of grasshoppers, and of Cecydes, and of the Buphonian festival! 985b Yet certainly these are those principles by which my system of education nurtured the men who fought at Marathon. But you teach the men of the present day, so that I am choked, when at the Panathenaia a fellow, holding his shield before his person, neglects Tritogenia, when they ought to dance. 990 Wherefore, O youth, choose with confidence, me, the better cause, and you will learn to hate the Agora, and to refrain from baths, and to be ashamed of what is disgraceful, and to be enraged if any one jeer you, and to rise up from seats before your seniors when they approach, and not to behave ill toward your parents, and to do nothing else 995 that is base, because you are to form in your mind an image of Modesty: and not to dart into the house of a dancing-woman, lest, while gaping after these things, being struck with an apple by a wanton, you should be damaged in your reputation: and not to contradict your father in anything; nor by calling him Iapetus, to reproach him with the ills of age, by which you were reared in your infancy. 1000 If you shall believe him in this, O youth, by Bacchus, you will be like the sons of Hippocrates, and they will call you a booby. 1002 Yet certainly shall you spend your time in the gymnastic schools, sleek and blooming; not chattering in the market-place rude jests, like the youths of the present day; nor dragged into court for a petty suit, greedy, pettifogging, knavish; 1005 but you shall descend to the Academy and run races beneath the sacred olives along with some modest compeer, crowned with white reeds, redolent of yew, and careless ease, of leaf-shedding white poplar, rejoicing in the season of spring, when the plane-tree whispers to the elm.

1036 And yet I was choking in my heart, and was longing to confound all these with contrary maxims. I will return, then, from thence to the tongue, which this fellow says our youths ought not to exercise, while I maintain they should. 1060 And again, he says they ought to be modest: two very great evils. Marry, he got a pretty piece of luck, the poor wretch! While Hyperbolus, he of the lamps, got more than many talents by his villainy, but by Jupiter, no sword! 1067 And Peleus married Thetis, too, through his modesty. 1068 And then she went off and left him; for he was not lustful, nor an agreeable bedfellow to spend the night with. 1070 Now a woman delights in being wantonly treated. But you are an old dotard. For (to Phidippides). consider, O youth, all that attaches to modesty, and of how many pleasures you are about to be deprived—of women, of games at cottabus, of dainties, of drinking-bouts, of giggling. And yet, what is life worth to you if you be deprived of these enjoyments? 1075 Well, I will pass from thence to the necessities of our nature. You have gone astray, you have fallen in love, you have been guilty of some adultery, and then have been caught. You are undone, for you are unable to speak. But if you associate with me, indulge your inclination, dance, laugh, and think nothing disgraceful. For if you should happen to be detected as an adulterer, you will make this reply to him, 1080 that you have done him no injury: and then refer him to Jupiter, how even he is overcome by love and women . And yet, how could you, who are a mortal, have greater power than a god? 1083 But what if he should suffer the radish through obeying you, and be depillated with hot ashes? What argument will he be able to state, to prove that he is not a blackguard? 1085 And if he be a blackguard, what harm will he suffer?
